question: SQ-LIP-000039
minor_problems: [minor] set: The central question (conversion of lipedema to lymphedema) has no clean proposition: P1 mixes the staging concept, mechanism and absence of cohort evidence, and the opposing 'distinct entity, not a precursor' view (E21, E17) is buried as a contradicting finding inside a supporting proposition.

[minor] set: E19 (lymphoscintigraphy normal in 61.4 percent, secondary lymphedema 11.8 percent) and E9 (no severe cases) are split between P1 and P2 and not reconciled with the 'many women' wording of P2.

[minor] set: P4 contains a claim ('not chronicity, stage or lymphoscintigraphic abnormality' / 'rather than disease duration') not found in the item text; role 'contradicting' does not match the proposition content.

[minor] P1: not fully supported; two ideas; misplaced ['E21', 'E17'] — suggested: Lipo-lymphedema is often described as an advanced stage or complication of lipedema, but longitudinal evidence that lipedema converts to lymphedema is lacking. (Bundles three ideas (described as a stage, attributed to lymphatic overload, no cohort evidence of conversion) and places the opposing view (E21 distinct entity, E17) inside a 'supporting' proposition. Staging reviews (E6, E7, E8, E12) restate a classification rather than evidence of conversion. E2 is a single post-surgical case. Hedged 'frequently described' so wording matches thin evidence. E9 (no severe cases, not necessarily progression) bears on this and sits under P2.)

[minor] P2: not fully supported; overgeneralized; two ideas; misplaced ['E19'] — suggested: Lymphatic transport abnormalities are reported in a substantial share of women with lipedema, often mild; their relation to stage remains uncertain. ('Usually mild' rests on E9 alone; E3 shows mean transport index above the pathologic threshold in severe disease. E19 (systematic review: lymphoscintigraphy normal in 61.4 percent) is the strongest item on prevalence of abnormality and is placed under P1; the 'many women' wording sits uneasily with it.)

[minor] P3: not fully supported; overgeneralized — suggested: Subclinical and clinical lymphedema in women with lipedema may be more frequent at higher body mass index, from limited cross-sectional data. (Single cross-sectional study (E5) with E15 a same-group review; no non-lipedema obese comparison, so the lymphedema may reflect obesity rather than lipedema progression. E20 (BMI change tracks volume change) is consistent.)

[minor] P4: not fully supported; overgeneralized; two ideas; stance errors ['E20'] — suggested: Limb volume in lipedema appears stable in most patients over several years, with volume change associated with changes in body mass index. ('Rather than disease duration' and the finding text 'not chronicity, stage or lymphoscintigraphic abnormality' are not in E20's quote or old_statement, which give only 62/28/10 percent stability and association with BMI and waist-to-height. Also role 'contradicting' is questionable: limb volume change does not address progression to lymphedema, and 28 percent progressed.)

[minor] P5: not fully supported; two ideas — suggested: Advanced stage or coexisting lipo-lymphedema may be associated with worse physical function in lipedema. (One survey of operated women (selection), weak correlation (r2 0.11), stage and lipo-lymphedema conflated. Hedged with 'may', so acceptable; E6 (immobility) not placed here.)

[minor] P6: not fully supported; overgeneralized — suggested: Coexisting lymphostasis may add a reducible fluid component to lipedema limbs, while adipose tissue persists after decongestive therapy. (A single case report generalised; hedged with 'may'. Peripheral to the question of progression.)

items.title: Lipedema

old_statements: In a systematic review of 7 studies (470 patients, 311 with lipedema), lymphoscintigraphy was normal in 61.4% of lipedema patients, with tortuous lymph vessels (56.8%), collateral vessels (49.1%), and popliteal node visualization (44.0%) as the most common abnormalities and dermal backflow rare (3.8%), reflecting lymphatic overload rather than frank insufficiency.

propositions.statement: Lipo-lymphedema is frequently described as an advanced stage or complication of lipedema attributed to chronic lymphatic overload, though cohort evidence of conversion is lacking.
propositions.rationale: Support is a consensus that itself flags lipolymphedema as an evidence gap, reviews, a pilot imaging study and one case; no cohort tracks conversion of lipedema to lymphedema, and one review rejects the link.

evidence.finding: Delphi consensus agreed lipolymphedema is a complication (3.95, level B) and lymph stasis is more evident in advanced stages (4.36), while flagging lipolymphedema as an evidence gap.

NIRF imaging in early-stage lipedema: dilated vessels and increased propulsion without dermal backflow; lymphatic failure absent in early disease but likely contributes to progression to lipolymphedema.
Systematic review (311 lipedema patients): lymphoscintigraphy normal in 61.4%; secondary lymphedema in 11.8% and dermal backflow in 3.8%, pattern read as overload rather than insufficiency.
Case report of a man with lipedema and post-surgical limb lymphedema: over 3 years, progression from subclinical to clinical systemic lymphedema by bioimpedance.
Review states advanced lipedema can obstruct lymphatics and cause secondary lymphedema documented by lymphoscintigraphy, with lymphatic microaneurysms seen even early.
Review describes lipedema as progressive, advancing to stage IV lipolymphedema with dorsal foot edema and positive Stemmer sign, leading to immobility.
Review describes four stages, stage IV being lipolymphedema with positive Stemmer sign.
Review describes four progressive stages culminating in stage 4 lipolymphedema, noting it is unclear whether lymphatic dysfunction is cause or consequence.
Systematic review characterizes lipedema as a distinct, progressive condition requiring early recognition, without quantifying progression to lymphedema.
Five women with early lipedema had concurrent early-stage lymphedema at enrolment in a physical therapy study (pain VAS 4.6 to 0.0 after therapy).
Among 250 lymphedema referrals, 9 lipedema patients showed symmetric foot-sparing swelling and negative Stemmer sign, framed as an entity distinct from lymphedema.
Review frames lipohyperplasia dolorosa and lymphedema as completely different disease entities, lipedema being a fat distribution disorder rather than a precursor of lymphedema.

propositions.statement: Lymphatic transport abnormalities are reported in many women with lipedema and are usually mild; whether they worsen with stage remains uncertain.
propositions.rationale: Abnormalities appear across all stages and are mostly low grade; the only stage gradient comes from one small study.

evidence.finding: In 83 patients, lymphoscintigraphic alterations in 47% across all stages including stage 1, mostly low or low-moderate grade, none severe.
Lymphoscintigraphy in 19 patients: pathologic transport (TI >10) in 63.2% of limbs; higher TI in stage 3/4 than stage 1/2 (15.1 vs 9.7, p=0.049).
Review reports abnormal lymphoscintigraphic patterns and impaired lymphatic transport already in early stages, without quantifying progression to lymphedema.
Review cites impaired lymphatic transport in lipedema but notes it lacks the T-cell inflammatory signature and lymphatic architectural changes of lymphedema, with fluid arising late.

propositions.statement: Lymphedema in people with lipedema is reported to be more frequent at higher body mass index.
propositions.rationale: Rests on one cross-sectional series (E5), re-reported by the same group's review (E15); cross-sectional data cannot show change over time.

evidence.finding: In 258 women, subclinical and clinical lymphedema were more frequent with higher BMI (<30: 16.3% and 6.1%; 30-40: 48.3% and 51.6%; 40-50: 72.2% and 77.8%; p=0.0001); edema also at normal weight.
Review by the same group proposes that lipedema patients, including BMI <30, develop systemic lymphedema that worsens and spreads to trunk and arms as obesity develops.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Subclinical and clinical lymphedema in women with lipedema is reported to be more prevalent at higher body mass index.

propositions.statement: Limb volume in lipedema appears stable in most patients over several years, with volume change associated with changes in body mass index.
propositions.rationale: A prospective cohort found most patients stable and linked volume change to BMI and waist-to-height gains, not to lymphoscintigraphic abnormalities.

evidence.finding: In 100 patients over 4.6 years, 62% stable, 28% progressed, 10% improved (mean volume change 2.8%); change associated with BMI and waist-to-height increases.

propositions.statement_before_arbitration: Lipedema limb volume may remain stable over years in most patients, with change tracking weight gain rather than disease duration.

propositions.statement: Functional impairment in lipedema appears to worsen with advancing stage and lipolymphedema, though quantitative data are limited.
propositions.rationale: One survey of operated women shows a weak inverse correlation, confounded with stage; limb volume is not addressed here.

evidence.finding: Survey of operated women: stage and lipo-lymphedema inversely correlated with LEFS function score (r2=0.11, P=0.0001); stage 1/2 scored higher than lipo-lymphedema.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Advanced stage or coexisting lipo-lymphedema may be associated with worse physical function in lipedema.

propositions.statement: Coexisting lymphostasis may add a reducible fluid component to limb volume in lipedema, while the adipose accumulation persists.
propositions.rationale: A distinct idea from one case, hence hedged.

evidence.finding: Case with lipedema and grade I lymphedema: lymph drainage and compression cut leg volume 10.6% and 6.78% in 3 days while lipedema fat remained.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Coexisting lymphostasis may add a drainable fluid component to lipedema limbs, while the adipose accumulation itself persists after drainage.

set_issues.issue: The central question (conversion of lipedema to lymphedema) has no clean proposition: P1 mixes the staging concept, mechanism and absence of cohort evidence, and the opposing 'distinct entity, not a precursor' view (E21, E17) is buried as a contradicting finding inside a supporting proposition.
